cells.tense: You're at the threshold with your eyes open, carrying only what matters.
cells.ask: Name what you're keeping and what you're letting go, out loud, to one person this week.
cells.core:
You can hold the whole shape at once right now — what drew you in, what stopped, and which pieces are worth carrying. Most people either cling or bolt. You're doing neither. You're unhurried in the middle of it, and that steadiness is why the next step will be clean instead of a scramble.

Because it's clear enough to see, it can be said out loud. Tell one person what you're taking with you and what you're setting down, and let them hear it without rushing to fix it. Something decided in front of someone else belongs to both of you, not just to you. That is how the bond survives the change.

cells.tense: You're bracing for a door that hasn't come into view yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you'd leave behind and actually leave it for a week, no announcement and no clean speech.
cells.core:
The leaving has gotten ahead of the living. You can see the next part so clearly you've started narrating it — preparing the closing remarks, rehearsing the reasons, bracing for a threshold that isn't here. The pressure to move is coming from restlessness, not from readiness.

What's getting lost is the ordinary contact still available to you now. Set one thing down for a week without a speech about it, and notice what stays. Not a test of anyone else — a check on your own footing, so you can tell apart what you're actually done with from what you're merely impatient to escape.

cells.tense: You're standing at a doorway you already passed through, still holding the handle.
cells.ask: Write three things you understand now that you didn't before, and read them to someone who wasn't there.
cells.core:
The crossing already happened, and some part of you stayed behind in the old part. You completed something real — a connection got fully made, a season closed — and you've been describing it as still pending, because finishing it would mean you actually changed and can't go back.

What's absent isn't depth. It's the accounting. See the pattern of what you gathered and what you left, because that is what makes the next threshold walkable instead of a cliff. Write three things you understand now, and say them to someone who wasn't there. That's how a past crossing becomes something you carry rather than something you stalled at.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what this ending means to the people you're leaving.
cells.ask: Say to one person, once: 'This chapter is done, and I decided what to keep.'
cells.core:
You've been framing this ending as the group drifting, the timing being off, people growing apart — but you chose which conversations to stop returning and what story to tell about why. The integration is happening. The claim that it's yours isn't.

Underneath is something simpler than the story: you needed quiet, you took it, and now the truth wants a plain sentence. Say it to one person without cushioning it. Not as an accusation of yourself — just as ownership, the way you'd say you moved a chair. Then the threshold is yours to walk instead of something that happened to you.

attempts.check: The claim the record does not support: that the person has a specific room or trip or person behind the leaving — that would fill in the Too Little shadow, which the brief says not to do. A reader could reasonably say the threshold is internal, not a departure from anyone. The ask survives being wrong because it only asks for a small concrete act of finishing or naming, useful whether or not the read is exact. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line like 'the leaving was already decided' — grand, not kitchen-table, cut.
